feed.title: Stiven Catalyst
feed.subtitle: Stiven Catalyst is an independent publication about leadership, operations, people, systems and practical change.

entry.title: Management Review No. 110: The wait the customer feels
entry.summary: A baggage hall where a longer walk ended the complaints, bank customers timed on video, eight propositions on how waits feel, a newsboard and a wait clock, a waiting room where people felt forgotten, and a check at the desk.

entry.title: Management Review No. 109: When the customer turns aggressive
entry.summary: Threats and attacks from customers and the public: who is most at risk in Britain, where it happens in Germany, what the ILO convention asks of employers, a trial in seven hospitals, what to record, and a card for one area.

entry.title: Management Review No. 108: Online ratings: what a star is worth
entry.summary: Half a star in Seattle, what a point is worth to a hotel, three things the average hides, the J that nobody chose, the fakes, and a card for reading the month's reviews.

entry.title: Management Review No. 107: Decision fatigue: the hungry judges
entry.summary: The parole study everyone quotes, the order of the cases it overlooked, a rational judge in a simulation, three explanations for one curve, how to count your own decisions, and a card for the last hour of the shift.

entry.title: Management Review No. 106: AI that screens CVs: the test and the law
entry.summary: The same CV under different names, the group that lost most, what the AI Act asks of providers and employers, a result that turned around with one design choice, a way to test your own screen, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 105: Maintenance that fits how things fail
entry.summary: How airlines learned that overhauls did not control failures, six patterns of failure and the 4% bathtub, three questions and four tasks, what an age limit would cost an engine shop, what “a life of 2,000 hours” can mean, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 104: Someone to talk to: connection at work
entry.summary: One employee in five lonely on any given day, 148 studies of relationships and survival, the difference between people around you and people who support you, a study of loneliness and leaving, three questions, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 103: The learning curve: every repetition counts
entry.summary: Wright's 80 percent, a car plant whose defects fell from about 70 to 20 a car in eight weeks, why the curve follows doublings and not the calendar, the second shift that did not start from zero, what an organisation forgets, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 102: Overtime: the number that borrows from tomorrow
entry.summary: Three kinds of overtime and why only two lengthen the year, how much is worked in Germany, who works it unpaid, what long days and weeks do to safety, and a weekly overtime card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 101: Listening: what the other person takes away
entry.summary: What a manager's listening is linked to at work, how strong the evidence really is, the three parts of good listening, why a conversation can be undone by what happens after it, and a card for the follow-up.

entry.title: Management Review No. 100: Slips, trips and falls: the ordinary accident
entry.summary: Why the fall on the level is the most common accident, where it happens in Germany, a trial with free slip-resistant shoes, three layers of prevention, and a floor walk at the end of the shift.

entry.title: Management Review No. 99: Lifting and the back: technique is not enough
entry.summary: Postal workers who learned to lift, nine trials with 20,101 workers, what the law puts before training, where the hands are, and a card for one handling task.

entry.title: Management Review No. 98: Output per hour: how the number is made
entry.summary: What goes above the line and below it, output per hour across the OECD, which hours count as worked, one economy with two denominators, how to count a site's hours, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 97: How sure is the manager?
entry.summary: Finance chiefs' 80% ranges that held a third of the time, three ways of being too sure, 90% that came true 73% of the time, forecasters who learned calibration, and a card for keeping score.

entry.title: Management Review No. 96: Check the AI's sources before it goes out
entry.summary: Six court decisions that never existed, how often a chatbot invented its references, why a real citation can still mislead, what legal tools built to avoid it still got wrong, and a card for the check before sending.

entry.title: Management Review No. 95: The second check: what it catches
entry.summary: Two nurses and a planted error, thirteen studies of the double check, the errors a second person catches and those they repeat, what bedside scanning changed, the overrides that show where it is bypassed, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 94: Noise at work: the ear and the quieter costs
entry.summary: Hearing that does not come back, Germany's most recognised occupational disease, the steps at 80, 85 and 87 dB(A), what noise does to speech, attention and strain, how a shift's exposure is measured, and a card for the loud area.

entry.title: Management Review No. 93: Defaults: the choice nobody makes
entry.summary: One company that turned its savings form around, eleven European countries and their organ donor rules, a meta-analysis of 58 default studies, the three ways a default works, and a card for the defaults a manager sets.

entry.title: Management Review No. 92: Sick leave: what the rate hides
entry.summary: Why Germany's sick days jumped in 2022, why three sources give three numbers, why a few long absences make most of the days, what the electronic sick note changed, and the absence the rate does not show.

entry.title: Management Review No. 91: Asking for advice: the fear that misleads
entry.summary: Why people avoid asking, what the person asked actually thinks, when a question makes you look more able and when less, why more people say yes than we expect, and a card for asking well.

entry.title: Management Review No. 90: The shift handover: what gets lost
entry.summary: A valve that was not mentioned at Piper Alpha, fifteen handovers watched in a refinery, what a structured log changed, the I-PASS programme in 9 and then 32 hospitals, and a card for the handover.

entry.title: Management Review No. 89: Hours awake: the tired shift
entry.summary: What 17 and 24 hours awake did to performance in the laboratory, how errors rose with the number of 24-hour shifts, what changed when the long shifts went, why sleep in the last 24 hours matters, and a card for the roster.

entry.title: Management Review No. 88: The bullwhip effect: small waves, big swings
entry.summary: A board game where demand changes once, how the swing grows link by link, four rational causes and a human one, what shared stock data does, how to measure the swing, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 87: Injury rates: how a safety number is made
entry.summary: Why 200,000 hours, what OSHA counts as a case, US rates by industry for 2024, why a small site's rate jumps, what Europe's rates and a survey of health practitioners say the number hides, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 86: Using AI without losing the skill
entry.summary: Experienced endoscopists who found fewer adenomas on their own after working with AI, students who asked the chatbot for answers and felt fine, two ways a skill is lost, an aviation rule for flying by hand, and a card for the switch-off check.

entry.title: Management Review No. 85: Checklists: one list, two results
entry.summary: Nineteen items that came with fewer complications in eight hospitals, the same idea with no measurable effect in 101 others, six hospitals with one list and six results, how a list is built for use, and a card to review one.

entry.title: Management Review No. 84: Heat at work: not only in a heatwave
entry.summary: Warehouses, kitchens, vans and laundries, nine in ten exposures outside heatwaves, Europe's fast rise, the first days in the heat, Germany's steps at 26, 30 and 35 °C, and a card for the hot shift.

entry.title: Management Review No. 83: Estimate first, then discuss
entry.summary: Galton's ox at Plymouth, why one wild guess can spoil an average, three ways seeing others' answers weakens a crowd, when exchange helps, and a card for independent estimates.

entry.title: Management Review No. 82: Regression to the mean
entry.summary: Why the worst shift improves on its own and the best one slips: Kahneman's flight instructors, Galton's heights, how big the false improvement gets, a control group that got better without help, and a card.

entry.title: Management Review No. 81: Predictable schedules: the roster as a management tool
entry.summary: An experiment in 28 stores, how little notice hourly workers get, why the hours weigh more than the pay, four sides of a stable roster, five numbers to watch, and a card for the next roster.
